ABSTRACT: Controlling the morphology and composition of bimetallic nanoalloys is an effective way to tailor their catalytic activity/selectivity for a given chemical reaction. Herein, we demonstrate the tailoring of bimetallic copper (Cu)-palladium (Pd) nanoalloys with different morphologies and compositions for obtaining highly efficient electrocatalysts for the reduction of CO2 to CO. We further evaluate the catalytic performance of these Cu-Pd nanomaterials for the electrochemical conversion of CO2 to CO. In particular, the spherical Cu-Pd nanoalloys with Cu/Pd molar ratio of 1/0.3 have the highest Faradaic efficiency for CO conversion (93%), while the dendritic Cu-Pd nanoalloys have the highest Faradaic efficiency for H2 production (65.2%) via hydrogen evolution reaction at a polarized potential of −0.87 V. The balancing of the rate determining steps during CO2 conversion is a key factor for the observed activity/selectivity of Cu-Pd nanoalloys with different morphologies/compositions. The findings revealed in this study may shed some light on the design of cost-effective and efficient electrocatalysts for CO2 conversion to CO or to other useful hydrocarbons.
Keyword: copper-palladium; nanoalloy; electrocatalyst; CO2 reduction; Faradaic efficiency

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Emission of carbon dioxide (CO2) as greenhouse gas has been at the record levels and it is expected to rise higher in future decades due to the accelerated consumption of fossil fuel.1−3 In order to mitigate the growth of CO2 concentration and meet the energy demand, in recent years various strategies, such as thermal catalysis, photocatalytic and electrocatalytic reduction, have been developed to convert CO2 into sustainable fuels and chemicals. 4−7 Among these newly developed approaches for CO2 conversion, electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 in aqueous solution has garnered sustained research interest owing to its mild reaction condition and clean reaction process.2,3,8−12 However, in electrocatalytic reduction of CO2, more negative potentials than the theoretical values (i.e., overpotentials) are required to induce the reduction of CO2, where the kinetically preferred hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) would also lead to low current efficiency and poor catalytic selectivity.9,10,13−17 Therefore, it is imperative to develop highly efficient catalysts, which could inhibit HER, as well as improve the catalytic activity towards CO2 reduction at low overpotentials.
It is well known that the morphology of materials at nanoscale has a key effect on their catalytic performance.14,18−24 Therefore, controlling the morphology of nanomaterials has become an efficient way to improve their catalytic performance. For example, Sun et al. synthesized ultrathin gold (Au) nanowires with abundant edge sites by using 2 nm Au nanoparticles as seeds via a seed-mediated growth pathway,25 and they found that the Faradaic efficiency of the as-prepared Au nanowires for the reduction of CO2 to CO could reach 94% due to the existence of reactive edge sites on the surface of these nanowires. In addition, the intrinsically catalytic properties of nanomaterials, e.g., nanoalloys, could be conveniently tuned by changing their compositions. The composition engineering of nanoalloys would influence the d-band center of the active components due to the lattice mismatch and the electronic coupling induced by different work functions, resulting in alteration of binding energies of reactant molecules on the surface of catalyst.26−29 Following the seminal work by Peterson and Nørskov, where copper (Cu)-based catalysts were used to promote the electrochemical reduction of CO2, 30 researchers have started to produce various Cu-based binary catalysts, e.g., Cu-Au and Cu-Pd alloys for the reduction of CO2. 9,32,31−34 Unfortunately,

despite the continuous development efforts in the past years, the electrocatalytic selectivity of CO2-reduction over HER by existing Cu-based catalysts is still not satisfactory.
In this study, we tailor the morphologies and compositions of bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys for obtaining highly efficient electrocatalysts for selective reduction of CO2 to CO. Cu-Pd nanoalloys with spherical, concave cubic and dendritic morphologies are produced via a delicate control of galvanic replacement reaction (GRR) between Cu seeds and Pd2+ precursors. The as-proposed approach could also be used to control the compositions of spherical Cu-Pd nanoalloys by co-reducing Cu2+ and Pd2+ precursors at different Cu/Pd molar ratios. We further evaluate the catalytic performance of these Cu-Pd nanomaterials for the electrochemical conversion of CO2 to CO. In comparison with a number of recent studies depicting individual effect of size,31 composition,32 or alloying patterns in Cu-Pd catalysts on the CO2 conversion, 33 we herein focus our investigation on elucidating the decisive factors of the activity/selectivity of Cu-Pd nanoalloys for CO2 conversion to CO. Specifically, spherical Cu-Pd nanoalloys with Cu/Pd molar ratio of 1/0.3 show the highest Faradaic efficiency for CO conversion (93%) at a potential of −0.87 V, while the dendritic Cu-Pd nanoalloys exhibit the highest Faradaic efficiency for H2 production via HER (65.2%) at the same polarized potential. The balancing of the rate determining steps during CO2 conversion accounts for the observed activity/selectivity of Cu-Pd nanoalloys with different morphologies/compositions. The findings revealed in this study may shed some light on the design of cost-effective and efficient electrocatalysts for the conversion of CO2 to CO, which is a useful intermediate for oxygenated chemicals and hydrocarbons.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
2.1. Chemcials. Copper(II) acetylacetonate (Cu(acac)2, 97%), palladium(II) acetylacetonate (Pd(acac)2, 99%) and Nafion 117 solution (5 wt%) from Sigma-Aldrich, oleylamine (70%, technical grade) and N, N-dimethylformamide (>99.99%) from J&K Chemicals, potassium bicarbonate (>99.5%), methanol (>99%), ethanol (>99.7%), toluene (>99.5%), perchloric acid solution (70%) and formic acid (>88%) from Beijing Chemical Works, Vulcan XC-72 carbon powders from Cabot, and commercial Pd/C catalyst (20 wt% Pd on XC-72 carbon substrates)

from Johnson Matthey (JM) were used as received. Deionized water purified by a Milli Q water system was used as universal solvent for aqueous solutions.
2.2. Synthesis of Cu nanoparticles. In a typical synthesis of Cu nanoparticles, 0.2 mmol of Cu(acac)2 was added to 10 mL of oleylamine, and then brought to 180°C from room temperature in a three-necked flask under stirring. The solution was kept at 180°C for 2 h to reduce Cu2+ ions with oleylamine. After the reaction, the Cu nanoparticles formed were precipitated with methanol, collected by centrifugation and further purified by a methanol-toluene mixture with a volume ratio of 3/1. Finally, the obtained Cu nanoparticles were re-dispersed in 10 mL of toluene.
2.3. Synthesis of bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys with spherical, concave cubic and dendritic morphologies. For the synthesis of bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys with different morphologies, a two-step method based on galvanic replacement reaction was applied. Firstly, Cu nanoparticles were synthesized by reducing 0.2 mmol of Cu(acac)2 in 10 mL of oleylamine at 180°C. Then, a different amount of Pd(acac)2 was swiftly added under vigorous stirring (0.02 mmol for spherical Cu-Pd, 0.06 mmol for concave cubic Cu-Pd, and 0.16 mmol for dendritic Cu-Pd, respectively). The mixtures were kept at 180°C for 3 h to complete the replacement reaction between Cu seeds and Pd(acac)2 for obtaining bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys with different morphologies. After precipitation with methanol, collection by centrifugation, and washing by a methanol-toluene mixture with a volume ratio of 3/1, the as-formed Cu-Pd nanoalloys were finally re-dispersed in 10 mL of toluene. According to the morphology of the alloys, the spherical, cubic, and dendritic Cu-Pd products were labeled as Cu-Pd-S, Cu-Pd-C, and Cu-Pd-D, respectively.
2.4. Synthesis of spherical Cu-Pd alloy nanoparticles with different Cu/Pd molar ratios. The spherical Cu-Pd alloy nanoparticles with different Cu/Pd molar ratios were synthesized via a one-pot method in oleylamine. In detail, 0.2 mmol of Cu(acac)2 and 0.02 mmol, 0.06 mmol, or 0.16 mmol of Pd(acac)2 were added to 10 mL of oleylamine, and the mixtures were heated to 180°C and kept at same temperature for 3 h to form spherical Cu-Pd nanoalloys with Cu/Pd molar ratio of 1/0.1, 1/0.3, or 1/0.8, respectively. The alloy products were also precipitated with methanol, collected by centrifugation, and washed by a methanol-toluene

2.5. Catalyst characterizations. A JEOL JEM-2100F electron microscope operated at 200 kV was used to obtain the images of transmission electron microscopy (TEM), high-resolution TEM (HRTEM), and scanning TEM (STEM) of the bimetallic Cu-Pd alloy samples. An energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analyzer attached to the transmission electron microscope was used to determine the chemical compositions of the as-synthesized nanoalloys. A Bruker D8 diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 0.154056 nm) was used to characterize the crystal phases of the as-prepared Cu-Pd nanoalloys by recording their X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns. A Thermo Scientific K-Alpha X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to analyze the chemical states of the elements in the bimetallic Cu-Pd nanpalloys.
2.6. Electrochemical measurements. We employed a commonly used strategy to load Cu-Pd nanoalloys on Vulcan XC-72 carbon supports. We added a calculated amount of carbon powders to the toluene solution of the bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys, and after stirring the mixture for 8 h, we collected the carbon supported Cu-Pd nanoalloys (20 wt% Cu and Pd on carbon substrates) by centrifugation, washed them thrice with ethanol, and dried them at room temperature in vacuum.
All electrochemical measurements were carried out on a Bio-logic VMP3 potentiostat and conducted using methods we described in a previous study.35 In brief, we ultrasonically dispersed 5 mg of the carbon-supported nanoalloys into 1 mL of ethanol containing 0.05 mL of Nafion solution to form an ink, and then 0.1 mL of the ink was dispensed onto a glassy carbon electrode (GCE) with an area of 1 cm×0.5 cm to generate working electrode with a nominal catalyst loading of 0.2 mg cm-2 (the total mass of Cu and Pd metal) based on the total mass loading of Cu and Pd on carbon supports (20 wt%). Further, the Pd mass loaded on the work electrode could be calculated according to the original molar ratio of Cu/Pd.
The electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 was carried out in a gas-tight H-cell separated by Nafion 117, as shown in Figure S1a, b and c of Supporting Information (SI). Each

compartment contains 40 mL of electrolyte and 10 mL of gas headspace. The Pt mesh with areas of 0.25 cm2 and Ag/AgCl (saturated with KCl) electrode were used as the counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively. All potentials in this study were converted to values with reference to a reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) by E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.21 V + 0.0591 × pH. The electrolysis was conducted at room temperature in CO2 saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution (pH = 7.3) under atmospheric pressure. Before the electrolysis was performed, the KHCO3 solution was purged by CO2 for 30 min to saturate the electrolyte and remove the air in the reservoir. The linear sweep voltammograms (LSVs) were recorded from 0 to −1.07 V at 10 mV s-1 at room temperature. The electrolysis was controlled at the selected potentials under 500 rpm stirring, in which CO2 gas was delivered at an average rate of 10 mL min-1 and the effluent gas from the cathodic compartment was analyzed by gas chromatograph (SRI 8610C) equipped a helium ionization detector (HID) every 30 min. The KHCO3 solution after electrolysis was collected and analyzed on a NMR (Nuclear Magnetic Resonance, Bruker AVANCE III 600 MHz) spectrometer to quantify the formate. Specifically, 1 mL of the electrolyte was mixed with 1 mL of D2O and 0.1 mL of N,N-dimethylformamide as internal standard. The 1H spectrum was measured with water suppression using a pre-saturation method.
We conducted the cyclic voltammetric measurements at room temperature in a three-electrode cell with an Ag/AgCl electrode a Pt mesh (1 × 1 cm2) as reference and counter electrode, respectively. A 5-mm GCE was used as work electrode with a nominal catalyst loading of 25.5 µg cm-2 (the total mass of Cu and Pd). We performed the electrochemical CO stripping tests in 0.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte at a scan rate of 50 mV s -1 to determine the electrochemically active surface areas (ECSAs) of the bimetallic Cu-Pd alloy catalysts. Analogous to the CO stripping in other acidic electrolyte (0.1 M HClO4), 35 we firstly introduced CO into the 0.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte for 20 min to complete the adsorption of CO onto the catalyst. The excessive CO was purged out by high purity N2. Then we calculated the ECSAs of the bimetallic alloy catalysts with ECSAs = Q/(420G), where Q, G, and number (420) are the charge of CO desorption–electrooxidation in microcoulomb (µC), the total mass of Pd on the electrode, and the charge (µC cm−2) required to oxidize a monolayer of CO on the catalyst, respectively.

Besides the property of the bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys in catalyzing CO2 conversion, we also evaluated the catalytic performance of these Cu-Pd nanoalloys and commercial Pd/C catalyst for formic acid oxidation reaction. For these electrochemical measurements, we scanned a potential window (-0.004−1.2 V) at a scan rate of 50 mV s-1. The electrolyte is 0.5 M H2SO4 aqueous solution containing 0.5 M formic acid (HCOOH). The current densities were normalized by the ECSAs of the bimetallic Cu-Pd alloys and commercial Pd catalyst to obtain their specific activity.

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
3.1. Characterization of Cu seeds and bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys. A two-step method (Figure 1), which is based on galvanic replacement reaction (GRR), was applied to tailor the morphology of bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys. Cu seeds were firstly produced in oleylamine to initiate the GRR between Cu metal and Pd2+ ion precursors. The TEM and HRTEM images of Cu seeds were shown in SI Figure S2a and b, which clearly show that these seed particles have spherical morphologies. The histogram that indicating size distribution of the particles (SI Figure S2c) demonstrates the average size of these Cu seeds is ca. 10.8 nm.

By varying Cu/Pd molar ratios (1/0.1, 1/0.3, and 1/0.8) through changing the amount of Pd2+ precursors, bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys with different morphologies could be obtained, as schematically illustrated in Figure 1. (SI Figure S3c), respectively. The element mappings (Figure 2a3−a6 for Cu-Pd spheres, Figure 2b3−b6 for Cu-Pd cubes, and Figure 2c3−c6 for Cu-Pd dendrites) demonstrate the uniform distributions of Cu and Pd in these bimetallic products, suggesting their alloy nature. In the XRD patterns of concave cubic and dendritic Cu-Pd particles (SI Figure S4d and f, respectively), no isolated peaks corresponding to Cu and Pd phases are observed, also indicating the formation of Cu-Pd alloy nanoparticles. In addition, as observed in Cu-Pd alloy multipods,35 the XRD diffraction peaks of these bimetallic Cu-Pd products have an appreciable positive shift in comparison with that of Pd (or a negative shift in comparison with that of Cu) due to smaller lattice parameter of Cu (0.3615 nm) than that of Pd (0.3890 nm).36 Of particular note, for spherical Cu-Pd samples (Cu-Pd-S), besides the peaks
corresponding to alloy phase, the retaining of the peak at 2θ of 43.3° in their XRD pattern (SI Figure S4) may suggest the presence of unreacted Cu cores in the alloy particles.

Specifically, increasing Cu content in bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys could promote the positive shift for 3d binding energies of Pd. The increase in Pd 3d binding energies indicates a lowered d-band center of Pd catalysts, which could greatly affect their catalytic performance by weakening the chemisorption energy of reactant molecules on the surfaces of Pd atoms.9,38,39
According to the CO stripping curves (SI Figure S6), the electrochemically active surface areas (ECSAs) normalized by the mass of Pd are calculated to be 67.0 m2 g-1 for the commercial Pd/C catalyst, 30.5 m2 g-1 for Cu-Pd-0.1, 48.3 m2 g-1 for Cu-Pd-S, 41.8 m2 g-1 for Cu-Pd-0.3, 36.4 m2 g-1 for Cu-Pd-C, 35.3 m2 g-1 for Cu-Pd-0.8, and 43.4 m2 g-1 for Cu-Pd-D nanoalloys, respectively. In comparison with that of the commercial Pd/C catalyst with ca. 3.2 nm Pd particles on Vulcan XC-72 substrates, the smaller ECSAs of the Cu-Pd nanoalloys might be due to their larger particle sizes and the absorption of residual impurities on their surfaces. It is noteworthy that although Cu-Pd-D (Cu-Pd alloy dendrites) and Cu-Pd-C (Cu-Pd alloy cubes) have much larger particle sizes than those of the corresponding Cu-Pd alloy spheres, their ECSAs are comparable, especially for Cu-Pd-D with greater ECSAs than that of Cu-Pd-0.8 nanoalloys, indicating higher atomic utilization in concave nanocubes and nanodendrites than that in the nanospheres due to the ample active edge/corner atoms in the concave cubic and dendritic structures.35,40,41
3.3. Catalytic performance of bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys for CO2 conversion to CO. The electrocatalytic performance of these Cu-Pd nanoalloys with different morphologies and compositions for CO2 reduction were examined. Figure 4a shows the linear sweep voltammogram (LSV) curves of these bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys in CO2 saturated KHCO3 solution. As observed, the dendritic Cu-Pd nanoalloys (Cu-Pd-D) exhibit the highest current

However, this overall current density does not mean the catalytic activity for CO2 reduction, because of the contribution of HER. In order to investigate the selectivity and activity of these Cu-Pd nanoalloys for the reduction of CO2 to CO, the Faradaic efficiency of CO and H2 for these nanoalloys was determined. Figure 4b, c and d show the Faradaic efficiencies of Cu-Pd nanoalloys with the same Cu/Pd molar ratios and different morphologies, respectively. At applied potentials from −0.57 to −1.07 V, the Faradaic efficiencies of CO for these nanoalloys have a maximum value, which could be reached at the potential of −0.87 V. In particular, as shown in Figure 4e, the Cu-Pd-0.3 alloy sample has the highest Faradaic efficiency of CO throughout the applied potentials, which reaches the largest value of 93% at −0.87 V (55.6% for Cu-Pd-0.1, 70.5% for Cu-Pd-S, 48.5% for Cu-Pd-C, 85.8% for Cu-Pd-0.8, 30.8% for Cu-Pd-D, and 37.4% for the commercial Pd/C catalyst, respectively). The high electric current efficiency of CO for Cu-Pd-0.3 nanoalloys also predicts their low production of H2 through HER. As shown in SI Figure S7, at applied potentials from −0.57 V to −1.07 V, Cu-Pd-0.3 nanoalloys always have the lowest Faradaic efficiency of H2 (only 5.7% for the Faradaic efficiency of H2 at −0.87 V), suggesting their superior electrocatalytic selectivity for converting CO2 to CO. As shown in Figure 4f and SI Figure S8a, compared with other catalysts the Cu-Pd-0.3 nanoalloys exhibits the highest specific activity and mass activity (Pd base) in applied potentials (−5.1 mA cm-2 and -25.7 A g-1 for the specific activity and mass activity, respectively at −0.87 V), which also illustrates their highly efficient catalytic activity for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CO. In addition, as summarized in SI Table S1, the highly catalytic efficiency of Cu-Pd-0.3 for the reduction of CO2 to CO has outperformed previously reported results.

The active HER on concave cubic and dendritic Cu-Pd nanoalloys could be mainly attributed to their unique structure providing more active edge/corner sites. Actually, a number of studies have uncovered that the hierarchical structures, e.g., nanodendrites, multipods and concave nanocubes, could enhance the catalytic performance for HER by facilitating the dissociation of water, which is the rate determining step for HER in alkaline solution, and accelerating the electrocatalytic kinetics.42−45 Besides HER, some other electrochemical reactions could also be promoted by the nanoalloys with hierarchical structures.40,41,46−49 We examined the catalytic performance of the as-prepared bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys for the electrooxidation of formic acid. As shown in SI Figure S9, the Cu-Pd-C and Cu-Pd-D nanoalloys display higher peak current densities for the formic acid oxidation than those with spherical morphologies (1.00 mA cm-2 and 1.14 mA cm-2 for Cu-Pd-C and Cu-Pd-D, respectively), proving their better catalytic activity for the oxidation of formic acid. Moreover, the slower decay of cubic and dendritic Cu-Pd nanoalloys in chronoamperograms indicates their superior durability for formic acid oxidation (SI Figure S10). We examined the morphological changes of these catalysts after electrochemical measurements. As shown in SI Figure S11, although the concave and dendritic structure of Cu-Pd-C and Cu-Pd-D disappear after the conducting chronoamperograms at 0.3 V for 2 h (SI Figure S11b1 and b2), the remaining spherical particles still have well dispersion on the carbon substrates compared with their concave and dendritic counterparts before electrochemical measurements (SI Figure S11a1 and a2), which guarantees their relatively superior electrocatalytic performance for formic acid oxidation. Nevertheless, apparent agglomeration is observed for Cu-Pd-0.3 nanoalloy and commercial Pd/C catalyst after conducting chronoamperograms (SI Figure S11b3 and b4), in comparison with those before the electrochemical measurements (SI Figure S11a3 and a4). Especially for commercial Pd/C catalyst, the original Pd nanoparticles on carbon substrates have seriously agglomerated into some lumps, resulting in the worst durability for formic acid oxidation.
For these Cu-Pd nanoalloy catalysts, formation of formate is inhibited in the electrolysis (SI Table S2), and CO is almost the sole product of CO2 reduction. As documented in previous studies,9,10,32,50 the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CO in aqueous solution

mainly includes three steps. Specifically, CO2 should be firstly absorbed on the catalyst surface, and subsequently reduced by incoming electron and coupled with the protons to form COOH intermediates. Then, the absorbed COOH intermediates would react with another proton, producing the absorbed CO. Finally, the absorbed CO should be released from the surface of catalyst, which is a non-electrochemical process. The conversion of CO2 to COOH intermediates, usually suppressed by weak binding energy of COOH, and the desorption of CO, inhibited by CO strong binding energy, have been considered to be two rate determining steps in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CO in aqueous solution. As discussed in XPS analyses, alloying Pd with Cu would lower the d-band center of Pd because of the lattice strain effect and electronic coupling between them, resulting in decrease of binding energy of intermediates on the surface of alloy. However, the weakening effect not only applies for the chemisorption of CO, but also for the adsorption of COOH intermediates. Therefore, the d-band center of Pd in bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys should be lowered to an appropriate location, which could better balance the absorption of COOH intermediates and desorption of CO on the surface of the nanoalloys, favorable for electrocatalytic selectivity and activity to reduce CO2 to CO.

The magnified CO stripping curves of the spherical Cu-Pd nanoalloys (commercial Pd/C catalyst, Cu-Pd-S, Cu-Pd-0.1, Cu-Pd-0.3 and Cu-Pd-0.8) and their valence band spectra were shown in Figure 5a and b, respectively. Obviously, with the increase of Cu content in Cu-Pd nanoalloys, the d-band center of Pd gradually lowers, and the potential of CO stripping also shifts more to the lower value. As shown in Figure 5b, although Cu-Pd-0.1 nanospheres possess the lowest d-band center and the most negative potential of CO stripping, they exhibit the lowest Faradaic efficiency of CO (55.6% at −0.87 V) and the smallest CO partial current density (−1.83 mA cm-2 and 9.13 A g-1 at −0.87 V) in comparison with those of other spherical Cu-Pd nanoalloys. This is because the lowest d-band center of Pd not only weaken the binding energy of CO, but also reduced the chemisorption of COOH intermediates on the surface of nanoalloys, resulting in the poor conversion of CO2 to COOH and hence less absorbed CO. Instead, for the alloys with an appropriate composition, e.g., Cu-Pd-0.3, their suitable d-band center deliver the best selectivity and activity for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CO by balancing the absorption of COOH intermediates and desorption of the absorbed CO on their surfaces. As confirmed by SI Figure S8b for the chronoamperogram, the total current density delivered by Cu-Pd-0.3 alloy catalyst and the corresponding CO Faradaic efficiency per 1 h remains stable and does not have apparent decay within 8 h at −0.87 V. Different from the morphological evolution after formic acid oxidation reaction, as shown in SI Figure S11, the morphologies of Cu-Pd-C, Cu-Pd-D, Cu-Pd-0.3 and commercial Pd after electrochemical CO2 reduction at -0.87 V for 30 min (SI Figure S11c1-c4) are maintained (SI Figure S11a1-a4), ensuring their highly catalytic performance for CO2 reduction reaction.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, we demonstrated the tailoring of bimetallic Cu-Pd nanoalloys with different morphologies and compositions, and evaluated their performance as electrocatalysts for reducing CO2 to CO. Specifically, we found that spherical Cu-Pd nanoalloys with Cu/Pd

molar ratio of 1/0.3 have the highest Faradaic efficiency for CO conversion (93%), while the dendritic Cu-Pd nanoalloys have the highest Faradaic efficiency for H2 production via HER (65.2%) at polarized potential of -0.87 V. The balancing of the rate determining steps during CO2 conversion may account for the observed activity/selectivity of the Cu-Pd nanoalloys with different morphologies/compositions, and the findings might be helpful for designing cost-effective and efficient bimetallic electrocatalysts for CO2 conversion to CO or to other valuable hydrocarbons.
